en: The Scripture on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
He was accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas,
whose names were: the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Arrayed with All Virtues, the Bodhisattva Lion’s Gait, the Bodhisattva King of Unobstructed Pure Light,
the Bodhisattva Sovereign King on the Summit of the High Mountain, and the Bodhisattva Pure Light of Joyful Affection.
The Bodhisattva Light Obscuring Sun and Moon, the Bodhisattva Sublime Pure Beard, the Bodhisattva Body Emanating Lotus Light,
the Bodhisattva Brahma-Sovereign-King Sound, the Bodhisattva Playful World-Lion-King Sound,
the Bodhisattva Golden Pure Light Majestic Virtue, the Bodhisattva Soft Body, and the Bodhisattva Adorned with Golden Marks.
The Bodhisattva Śarīra, the Bodhisattva Daśaraśmimārapramardaka, the Bodhisattva Sarvendriyasaṃvṛtavinīta,
the Bodhisattva Guṇaparvata, the Bodhisattva Divyaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Dharmabalavikrāmiṇa,
the Bodhisattva Parvataguṇaviśuddhakāya, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suśīla; such were they.
[Accompanied by] ninety-two thousand people.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, seeing this great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and questioned him in verse:
“World-Honored One, Great Guide, Whose name and virtue are praised as immeasurable,
Now this great assembly has gathered; we pray that you will preach the Dharma of quiescence.
How can false views, craving, pride, envy, and the nature of anger be the very path?
The Great Sound explains through skillful means:
"What is the characteristic of nirvāṇa? It is no different from worldly phenomena.
All dharmas are non-dual; out of great compassion, he expounds this."
What is the nature of all phenomena, That they are ultimately without obstruction?
Their nature is like nirvāṇa, And likewise identical to liberation;
Neither bound nor liberated, They are also like empty space.
With a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, possessing the pure sound of Great Brahmā;
with a body colored like celestial gold, endowed with immeasurable virtues and a pure livelihood;
he expounds the Dharma of the true mark, which is ultimately neither bound nor liberated.
How can these five hindrances be equal to bodhi?
How can this bodhi be identical to the nature of all karmas?
How can that which is dharma and that which is non-dharma be of one and the same characteristic?
Thus it is ultimately pure; I only pray that you will expound upon this.
It is neither number nor non-number; all phenomena are ultimately extinguished.
The marks of the knowledge of all modes, as well as the path to enlightenment— Please explain these for me.
How is it that these two dharmas do not exist?
I pray that you will explain this for me:
there is no action and no non-action; there is no attachment and no non-attachment.
Ultimately there are no sentient beings; among all phenomena there is no obstruction.
There is no precept and no patience, nor is there any violation of precepts.
There is neither wisdom nor insight, nor is there anything that is not wisdom.
This Dharma is eternally pure; I pray that you will expound it for me.
How is it that all phenomena are as quiescent as empty space?
How is it that there is neither mind nor mental factors, and neither seeing, abandoning, realizing, nor cultivating?
All sentient beings are identical to the nature of space;
even this single characteristic of phenomena does not exist, nor can any mental activity be apprehended.
All dharmas are without arising or ceasing; there are no learners and no arhats.
There are no pratyekabuddhas, nor are there any who seek to be bodhisattvas;
there is no abiding and no cessation, no coming and no going.
All dharmas are devoid of the mark of movement, eternally abiding like Mount Sumeru.
Without marks and without form, the nature of form is itself the Path;
the nature of form and the Buddha-path are one—please explain such a Dharma.
Why is there no Buddha-dharma, and why is there also no Saṃgha?
These Three Jewels are of one single characteristic; I only pray that you will expound upon them for me.
There is no emptiness, no signlessness, and likewise no wishlessness;
they are neither conjoined nor dispersed, and even the names, characteristics, and dharmas do not exist.
All dharmas are ultimately empty, like echoes without an agent;
they are neither born nor unborn, neither extinguished nor coming and going;
there are no devas, no nāgas or spirits, no yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and the like.
There is no person, no hell, no hungry ghosts, no animals, and no sentient beings in the five realms; may you preach such a Dharma.
Like a guide for the world, you are not one who holds the views of external paths.
Regarding that which you have expounded—how is it that equality is non-dual?
All letters and languages are of a single characteristic within this Dharma;
O World-Honored One of great compassion, we pray that you will open this Dharma gate.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
"What you have asked is most rare and difficult for all the world to believe.
Good son! Desist, desist; do not ask."

Why is this? Because bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds cannot reach these views: the view of emptiness, the view of signlessness, the view of wishlessness, the view of non-arising, the view of non-existence, the view of non-apprehension of signs, the view of the Buddha, and the view of enlightenment.
Good son!
This Dharma should not be taught before bodhisattvas who are newly trained. Why is this?
If they hear this Dharma, they may sever their roots of goodness and thus proceed along a deviant path within the Buddha-way;
they may fall into the view of annihilationism or the view of eternalism, failing to understand by what skillful means the Tathāgata speaks in accordance with what is appropriate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for the world, we pray that you will surely explain this for us.”

In future ages, there will be bodhisattvas who hold views of emptiness, views of signlessness, views of wishlessness, views of non-arising, views of non-existence, views of non-apprehension of signs, views of the Buddha, and views of bodhi. Such people will discriminate, thinking, "This is emptiness; this is signlessness and wishlessness. They will delight in constantly praising study and diligence in worldly affairs, taking pleasure in literary composition and regarding eloquent speech as marvelous. Valuing fame and profit, when such people hear the Tathāgata teach this Dharma that is without words and ultimately pure, they shall abandon all these views.

These bodhisattvas, according to the capacity for faith and understanding of sentient beings, preach the Dharma through the power of skillful means. Although they speak of few desires and contentment, they do not regard this as supreme; although they speak of the sutras and precepts, they do not regard these as supreme; although they speak of the faults and evils of being in a crowd, they know that all phenomena possess the characteristic of detachment, and while they constantly praise dwelling alone rather than in clamor and bustle, they do not regard this as supreme.

Although they praise the arousal of the bodhicitta, they know that the nature of the mind is itself bodhi; although they praise the Mahāyāna sūtras, they know that all dharmas are the mark of the Great Vehicle; although they speak of the Bodhisattva path, they do not differentiate between arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas; although they praise giving, they penetrate the mark of the equality of giving; although they praise the observance of precepts, they understand that all dharmas are identical in their nature as morality; although they praise patience, they know that all dharmas have the mark of being unborn, unceasing, and inexhaustible; although they praise diligence, they know that all dharmas have the mark of neither arising nor proceeding; although they praise meditative concentration in various ways, they know that all dharmas are eternally in a state of concentration; and although they praise wisdom in various ways, they realize the true nature of wisdom.

Although they speak of the faults of desire, they do not perceive any dharma that is desirable; although they speak of the faults of hatred, they do not perceive any dharma that is hateful; although they speak of the faults of ignorance, they know that all dharmas are without delusion and without obstruction; and although they show sentient beings the suffering and terrors of falling into the three evil realms, they do not perceive the characteristics of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

In this way, although these bodhisattvas preach the Dharma by means of skillful power according to the capacities for faith and understanding of sentient beings, they themselves have confidence and understanding in the dharma of a single characteristic—namely, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-existence, and the absence of signs of grasping.
World-Honored One!

We only pray that you will expound this inconceivable Dharma of skillful means, which is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, but is taught solely for those who believe in and understand the profound Dharma of the single mark.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
"Good son, listen attentively now and reflect well upon it; I shall explain this meaning for you."
“Yes, World-Honored One!
I shall accept it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“If a person wishes to attain Buddhahood, Do not destroy desire;
all dharmas are themselves desire. To know this is to attain Buddhahood.”
Greed, anger, and delusion—none can ever obtain them;
these phenomena are all like space, and knowing this, one attains Buddhahood.
To see and not to see are of one and the same mark; so too are attachment and non-attachment.
Here there is no Buddha and no Dharma; to know this is called great wisdom.
Just as a person in a dream attains the Way and delivers sentient beings—yet there is neither Way nor sentient beings—the nature of the Buddha-Dharma is likewise so.
The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is without anything to be attained; if it were attained, it would not exist.
Wisdom and ignorance are of one single mark—knowing this is to be the World-Honored One.
Sentient beings are themselves bodhi; bodhi is itself sentient beings.
Enlightenment and sentient beings are one; To know this is to be a World-Honored One.
Just as a skilled illusionist Manifests various things through illusion, What is seen has no reality, Yet the ignorant reckon them as many.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are like illusions; illusions are not different from the three poisons.
It is only through their own conceptualization that ordinary beings think, "I am greedy," or "I am hateful.
Such foolish people will fall into the three evil realms.
In the true nature of reality, there is no greed or hatred, nor can delusion be found;
yet by discriminating phenomena as being like illusions, one generates the fever of afflictions oneself.
In the true nature of reality, there are no afflictions, no sentient beings, and no Buddhas.
Discriminating the dharma of non-arising, ordinary beings vow to become Buddhas.
Not seeing the dharmas of the Buddhas, nor seeing sentient beings—
those who know the characteristics of these dharmas will swiftly become Honored Ones among sentient beings.
If a person seeks awakening, then there is no awakening;
such a person is far from awakening, like the distance between heaven and earth.
One who knows that all phenomena are like illusions will swiftly become the supreme among men.
If a person discriminates regarding the precepts, they possess no precepts at all;
if there is one who views the precepts as a fixed entity, they have lost the precepts.
That the precepts and non-precepts share a single characteristic—knowing this is to be a teacher.
Like experiencing the five desires in a dream, one finds pleasure and joy;
yet through discrimination one perceives female forms, though in reality there is no woman therein.
So it is with the precepts and their violation—like a dream—yet the ordinary person discriminates between the two.
In reality, there is neither precept nor violation of precepts; one who knows this is a teacher.
Ordinary people are attached to names and do not know the nature of language.
Names are not names; one who knows this attains the state of non-arising.
Claiming for oneself to be a bodhisattva, one recites and explains the teachings to others;
yet one practices nothing oneself, relying solely on one's noble lineage.
Merely reading the scriptures in search of the Way, one constantly observes the faults of others.
Those who compose verses on outward decorum, seeing others respect them and thus regarding themselves as noble;
those who rely on their lineage and compose verses, yet do not know the true nature of phenomena—
such persons as these will ultimately never attain Buddhahood.
For them, he teaches that all phenomena are empty;
those with malicious minds who delight in contention possess neither the Buddha-dharma nor awakening.
Knowing that anger and patience share the same nature, one who realizes this will never again give way to anger.
Failing to understand the nature of sentient beings, they give rise to anger.
Claiming for themselves to be bodhisattvas, they further speak thus:
"I am compassionate toward all; I shall attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings."
Provoked by resentment, he gives rise to anger; harboring indignation, he does not speak with others.
He constantly seeks out the faults of others and delights in strife and litigation;
yet he also praises patience and speaks of the emptiness of all phenomena.
My mind is full of arrogance; I constantly observe the faults of others, am greedily attached to delicious flavors, and day and night contemplate the five desires.
Such a person enters a city or town and claims, "I am one who delivers others."
With compassionate thoughts for sentient beings, always seeking their benefit,
though such words may issue from the mouth, the heart delights in troubling others.
I have never seen or heard of one who practices compassion while acting with malice.
If one harbors mutual anger and resentment toward others, yet vows to be born in Amitābha’s land;
or if there are people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who assail one with harsh words, swords, and staves—
if one can endure all such things, then one shall be born in the Pure Land.
The Buddha-field is not a Buddha-field; knowing it to have the characteristic of space, one does not discriminate between lands or the merits of those lands.
Such persons as these are able to be born in the realms of all Buddhas.
They claim to endure all evils and regard Bodhisattvas as Buddhas;
yet I have never seen or heard of one who, while possessing the marks of a Buddha, would harbor anger.
Each praises themselves and slanders others, taking pleasure in donors and acquaintances.
I say that those whom I have taught and protected so that they act according to the Dharma—
those you should approach for deliverance— do not associate with others;
for their conduct is impure and they constantly dwell in the clamor of the world.
Such a person will be unable to diligently practice the Buddha-way.
One who truly seeks the Buddha-way should, three times each day and night,
prostrate to all Bodhisattvas and give rise to a heart of reverence.
One should not speak of the faults of those who follow their own path;
even if one sees them attached to the five desires, one should not speak of their transgressions.
One should instead reflect that such persons will also attain the Way after a long time.
The path of practice proceeds by stages; one cannot attain Buddhahood instantaneously.
Or perhaps it is because they have not long since resolved their minds [on enlightenment] that they must perform these practices.
Do not discriminate against desire; the very nature of desire is the Path.
Afflictions did not exist previously, nor will they exist in the future;
one who can believe and understand in this way attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Observing pleasant and unpleasant sounds, one knows they do not have the nature of sound.
When entering the dharma-gate of the signless reality,
if one can have faith in this teaching, then there will be no lust, anger, or delusion.
To contemplate greed, desire, and ignorance is itself the mark of the immeasurable.
These two are without words; they are spoken of by means of words.
All places where words exist are entirely devoid of reality.
All sounds and voices should be contemplated as having the nature of a single sound.
The Buddha’s teachings and false doctrines—these are all without distinction.
Although the Dharma is expressed through words, in reality there is neither Dharma nor speech.
One who can enter the gate of the single characteristic attains supreme patience.
"This is patience; this is not patience"—do not make such distinctions.
Regarding the minds of desire and hatred, do not calculate any benefit therein.
Knowing that these two are non-arising, you shall become the Honored One in the world.
In the directions of east, west, south, and north, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,
were all ground into fine dust; each particle of dust became a world,
filled with every kind of precious jewel, for incalculable eons.
The merit obtained from making offerings to all the Tathāgatas—
if a person hears this sutra, it shall exceed that by hundreds of thousands of times.
If there is a renunciant who single-mindedly seeks the Buddha-way,
I entrust this person with this secret and essential dharma.
If there are those who recite this sutra and understand its meaning,
they shall naturally attain immeasurable dhāraṇīs and eloquence.
With sharp faculties and inexhaustible wisdom, and the eloquence of joyful speech,
all the immeasurable billions of Buddhas likewise grant this person the wondrous Dharma-treasures of the various sutras, so that they may naturally expound them all.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these verses now spoken, how many people will attain their own benefit?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son! Do you see this great assembly?"
“Yes, I have seen it.
The Buddha said:

“Now, as this Dharma is being taught, there has gathered in this assembly an immeasurable and incalculable number of sentient beings. Together with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, and others, they fill the void of space. Through the brilliance of this teaching of the Dharma, many will be benefited even in worlds in other directions.”
Ninety-two thousand yakṣa deities all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Five hundred bhikṣus of overweening pride—who had not attained [realization] yet claimed they had—upon hearing this Dharma, were freed from overweening pride; they attained true faith in the Dharma, understood that all dharmas are of a single characteristic, and because they did not grasp at any dharmas, their outflows were exhausted and they attained liberation.

Thereupon, among the assembly of bodhisattvas, sixty-two thousand people, having gained faith and understanding in the unobstructed nature of all dharmas, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Why was this?
This teaching of the Dharma is the foremost among all teachings of the Dharma. Good son!

Just as I, in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, attained the realization that all dharmas are of one mark and unimpeded, and only thereafter did I obtain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and become fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*.

Why is this? If a bodhisattva, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, practices giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, yet does not understand such characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa), that person may even sever all roots of goodness.
"Good son!

You see that Devadatta possessed great merit and roots of goodness, having accomplished the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; yet, because he did not understand such characteristics of dharmas despite possessing such merit, he severed his roots of goodness and fell into the great hells."

“Good son! You should know that although one may have long since resolved upon enlightenment and possess great merit, if one does not enter this Dharma-gate, all roots of goodness and merit will be severed and extinguished.”
"Good son!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Sumeruśikhara-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His lifespan was nine thousand nine hundred ten-million-billion *nayuta* years, and his land was named Suvarṇajvālāprabhā; that land had the ground entirely made of gold."
The Dharma he teaches likewise delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. At his first assembly, there are eighty hundred thousand million billion nayutas of śrāvaka disciples;
at the second assembly, seventy hundred thousand million billion nayutas of śrāvaka disciples;
and at the third assembly, sixty hundred thousand million billion nayutas of śrāvaka disciples.
In the fourth assembly, there were fifty hundred thousand million billion nayutas of śrāvaka disciples;
all had attained arhatship, laid down their heavy burdens, achieved their own welfare, exhausted the fetters of existence, and attained liberation through right knowledge.

The assembly of bhikṣuṇīs was twice that number; the assembly of upāsakas was also twice that number; the assembly of upāsikās was also twice that number; and the assembly of bodhisattvas was also twice that number. All of them had attained the non-retrogressive patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and had all attained immeasurable and boundless dharanī-gates and samādhi-gates, being able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma—how much more so those who had newly resolved their minds toward awakening!
Furthermore, those who have resolved to attain the path of a *pratyekabuddha* are also immeasurable and boundless. "Good son!

At that time, the number of disciples in that Buddha’s assembly was immeasurable and boundless. In that land of Golden Flame, all trees were made of the seven treasures; from those jewel-trees there constantly issued forth the sounds of the Dharma—namely, the sound of the emptiness of all phenomena, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-existence, and the sound of the absence of grasping at signs."
When the people of that land heard this sound of the Dharma, they all spontaneously attained the true mark of all phenomena and their minds achieved liberation.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma remained for a thousand years, and the sounds from the various jewel trees no longer issued forth.
"Good son!

This Tathāgata Sumeruśikhara entrusted the Dharma to the Bodhisattva Viśuddheryāpatha, commanding him to protect and uphold it; having thus made his entrustment, he entered parinirvāṇa without remainder."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Yiwéi (Uddhata). Although his observance of the precepts was impure, he had attained the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers; he was well-versed in reciting the Vinaya Piṭaka, delighted in ascetic practices, yet was unable to skillfully know the minds of others.
His assembly of disciples likewise all practiced asceticism and esteemed the dhūta-precepts.
This Dharma Master Viśuddheryāpa was pure in his observance of the precepts and attained skillful means within the dharma of non-existence.

Again, at one time, the Dharma Master Pure Conduct took his disciples and went to the residence of the Bhikṣu Noble Conduct to dwell together with him. Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Dharma Master Pure Conduct would regularly enter the villages from his place of residence after meals and return; he converted hundreds of thousands of households, making them all his disciples and causing them to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

His assembly of disciples was also well-trained in teaching and transformation; they traveled to various villages and preached the Dharma for them, causing hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to all resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

There was a bhikṣu of dignified demeanor who always delighted in dwelling at stūpas and monasteries; his assembly of disciples did not maintain the pure precepts, yet they delighted in practicing the dhūtas.

This bhikṣu of dignified demeanor practiced with diligence and resolute mind, seeking to transform his disciples through his own conduct. He was attached to wholesome dharmas and held specific views and attainments, namely that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and suffering, and that all phenomena are without self. However, he was unable to skillfully practice the methods of dhyāna and samādhi, nor was he skilled in the path practiced by bodhisattvas, because his original mind was not pure.

The Dharma Master Pure-Demeanor (Śuddheryāpatha) well understood the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings; because he knew the mind of the monk Upananda, he no longer regularly entered the village, yet his disciples remained exactly as they were before, without any change.

A bhikṣu of dignified deportment, seeing that the disciples of the Dharma Master Viśuddha-īryāpatha constantly entered villages and giving rise to impure thoughts, struck the *ghanṭī* to assemble the community and established a regulation:
"From this day forward, you should not enter villages; for what benefit do you gain by frequently entering villages without being able to walk slowly and in silence with a single-minded focus?"
"The Buddha has praised dwelling in forest hermitages; you should practice the joy of meditation and not take pleasure in entering the homes of others.
Yet the disciples of the Dharma Master Viśuddheryāpatha did not heed his words and continued to enter the villages.
Later, on one occasion, there was a bhikṣu of dignified demeanor who saw [the monks] coming out from the village; he struck the *gaṇḍī* again to assemble the community and spoke these words:
"If any of you enter the village again, you shall no longer be permitted to remain here."
At that time, the Dharma Master Viśuddheryāpa, in order to protect the bhikṣus of proper deportment, told his disciples: "You all!
From this day forward, do not enter villages."
He then followed his teacher’s instruction and did not enter the village.
At that time, because the people did not see their teacher or his disciples, they all harbored grief and distress, and their roots of goodness declined and were lost.

After the Dharma Master Viśuddheryāpa has completed the three-month period and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he departs from there for another monastery; he and his disciples then enter cities, towns, and villages to preach the Dharma to people.

Later, there was a bhikṣu of dignified deportment who saw the Dharma Master Viśuddheryāpa entering another's house; seeing that the master’s disciple had violated his regular decorum, he conceived an impure and evil thought, thinking:
"This bhikṣu has broken and ruined the precepts; how can there be any bodhi for him?"
He then said to the assembly:
"This bhikṣu practices in a mixed manner; he is very far from the Buddha-way.

After this bhikṣu of majestic deportment had given rise to such karma, he later passed away. Due to the retribution of that karma, he fell into the Avīci Great Hell and underwent various sufferings for nine hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas.
After emerging from hell, he was subjected to constant slander for six hundred and thirty thousand lifetimes.

As his transgressions gradually thinned, he later became a bhikṣu for three hundred and twenty thousand lifetimes; yet after leaving the home life, due to the causal conditions of those karmic deeds, he turned back from the Way and returned to secular life. Furthermore, because of the remaining causes and conditions of his sinful karma, although he left the home life and entered the Path under the Buddha Vimalaprabha, practicing with such diligent vigor as if extinguishing a fire on his head, he did not attain the patient endurance of accordance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) throughout ten million *koṭis* of years. For immeasurable thousands of millions of lifetimes, his faculties remained dull and obtuse.
“Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, what do you think?
Was that bhikṣu of majestic deportment at that time someone else?
Do not entertain such a thought; it was none other than myself.”
At that time, because I gave rise to such a subtle and impure thought, I incurred this karmic retribution and fell into hell.
Siṃhavikrāntagāmin!
If a person does not wish to give rise to such subtle offenses, they should not harbor ill will toward that bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva should have faith and understanding in all the paths they practice; they should not give rise to a mind of anger or resentment, but should instead think:
"I cannot skillfully know the minds of others, and the conduct of sentient beings is likewise difficult to know."

“Good son! Because the Tathāgata perceives such benefit, he constantly teaches this Dharma; therefore, a practitioner should not judge others superficially. Only the Tathāgata and those who resemble the Tathāgata can truly know this.”
Therefore, if a practitioner wishes to protect their own person, they must be careful not to judge others or act in opposition to them.
If a bodhisattva wishes to cultivate and accumulate the Buddha-dharma, they should always, day and night, apply themselves with diligence and single-minded mindfulness.
Those who have deeply resolved to attain the Bodhisattva mind should not delight in seeking out the faults of others.

If a Bodhisattva were to teach all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm to practice the ten wholesome paths of action, it would not equal the merit of another Bodhisattva who, for the duration of a single meal, dwells with a single-minded focus in a quiet place, contemplating the Dharma-gate of a Single Characteristic, or even hearing, receiving, reading, reciting, and explaining it; the latter’s merit far surpasses that of the former by a great measure.

Why is this? Because by means of this Dharma-gate, all Bodhisattvas are able to extinguish all karmic obstructions and transgressions, and they are also able to remain free from feelings of aversion or attachment toward any sentient beings; thus, they can swiftly attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the Buddha has taught concerning the extinguishing of karmic obstructions and offenses—how does one extinguish these karmic obstructions and offenses?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If a bodhisattva perceives that the nature of all dharmas is without karma and without retribution, they will be able to completely extinguish the offenses of karmic obstructions.”
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If a bodhisattva perceives the limit of greed as the true limit, the limit of hatred as the true limit, and the limit of delusion as the true limit, they will be able to completely extinguish the offenses of karmic obstructions.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If a bodhisattva can see that the nature of all sentient beings is itself the nature of nirvāṇa, they will be able to completely extinguish the offenses of their karmic obstructions.

Why is this so? If a person has their own views, they are immediately able to initiate karma. Ignorant and unlearned ordinary fools do not know that all phenomena have the characteristic of ultimate cessation; therefore, they perceive their own bodies and perceive others. Because of these perceptions, they give rise to actions of body, speech, and mind.
This person, through false views, recollections, and conceptual discriminations, forms this thought:
"I am desire, hatred, and delusion.
Because of such discrimination, they leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma to study the Path, yet again form this thought:
"I am one who upholds the precepts and practices the holy life; I shall transcend birth and death, attain nirvana, and be freed from all suffering and affliction.

This person discriminates among phenomena, thinking: "This is wholesome, this is unwholesome; this should be known, this should be abandoned, this should be realized, and this should be cultivated"—namely, that suffering should be seen, its origin should be abandoned, its cessation should be realized, and the path should be cultivated.

Furthermore, he discriminates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are entirely suffering, and all conditioned phenomena are ablaze with the three poisons; "I shall quickly abandon these conditioned dharmas."
Constantly reflecting in this way, one gives rise to a mind of revulsion by perceiving various signs within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
At that time, one forms this thought:
"To see all conditioned phenomena in this manner is called 'seeing suffering' (*duḥkha-darśana*)."
"To feel revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is called the abandonment of the origin [of suffering].
Distinguishing all conditioned phenomena, one perceives the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya) and immediately forms this thought:
'I have now seen cessation; this is called the realization of cessation. I shall cultivate the Path.'"
He then went to a quiet place and contemplated this Dharma; having made this reflection, he gathered his mind and remained in meditative concentration.

This person had previously attained a mind of revulsion, and now he has attained a concentrated mind; therefore, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), his mind becomes detached. Feeling self-reproach and weariness, neither finding joy nor pleasure, he further reflects:
"I have now attained liberation within all dharmas; there is nothing more to be done. My body has already realized the path of an Arhat."

When this person’s life comes to an end, they see the place where they are to be reborn; at that moment, doubt and regret arise within their bodhicitta, and because of this doubt, after death they fall into the great hells.
"Why is this? Because these people engage in conceptual discrimination regarding dharmas that are non-arising.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one now contemplate the Four Noble Truths?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If a practitioner is able to see that all phenomena are of the nature of non-arising, this is called seeing suffering.
If they are able to see that all phenomena neither accumulate nor arise, this is called abandoning the origin."
If one can see that all phenomena possess the characteristic of ultimate cessation, this is called realizing cessation (*nirodha*).
If one can see that all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, this is called cultivating the path (*mārga*).

Mañjuśrī! If a practitioner can see the Four Noble Truths in this way, that person does not make such distinctions as: "this dharma is wholesome" or "this dharma is unwholesome"; "this dharma should be seen," "this dharma should be abandoned," "this dharma should be realized," or "this dharma should be cultivated"—namely, that suffering should be seen, origination should be abandoned, cessation should be realized, and the path should be cultivated.

Why is this so? Because the ordinary person practices greed, hatred, and delusion, whereas the practitioner perceives these phenomena as all empty, unarisen, non-existent, and beyond conceptual differentiation—being merely accumulations of falsehood.

At that time, one neither grasps nor rejects anything regarding phenomena; the mind is unimpeded within the three realms, seeing that all three realms are ultimately non-arising, and seeing that all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are deceptive and unreal, like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, an echo, or a mirage.
The practitioner perceives that the nature of desire is itself the nature of nirvana; the nature of hatred is itself the nature of nirvana; and the nature of delusion is itself the nature of nirvana.
If one can see the nature of all phenomena in this way, one will not give rise to hatred or attachment toward any sentient beings. Why is this?

Because this practitioner does not apprehend these phenomena—whether in a place where love arises or a place where hatred arises—they abide in emptiness like space. Within their mind, they do not even perceive the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha; thus, they do not perceive any phenomena at all.

If one does not perceive all phenomena, then doubt will not arise regarding those phenomena. Because doubt does not arise, one does not grasp at any phenomena. Because one does not grasp at any phenomena, there is spontaneous quiescence.
Mañjuśrī! Because the Elder Subhūti understands such dharmas, he does not come to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
Subhūti does not even apprehend his own body, let alone apprehend the body of a Tathāgata.
"It is impossible that one could attain the body of a Tathāgata without first attaining one's own [true] body.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How should a practitioner contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“In a future age, there will be bhikṣus who speak in this way:”

"To contemplate the internal body as impure is the foundation of mindfulness of the body; to contemplate all that is pleasant as suffering is the foundation of mindfulness of sensation; to contemplate the nature of the arising and ceasing of the mind is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and to contemplate the dissolution of compounded phenomena until only the characteristics of dharmas are attained is the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How, now, does one truly contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness?”
The Buddha said:
"Stop, stop, Mañjuśrī!"
"There is no need to ask; the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One!"
“Out of compassion for sentient beings, I pray that you will certainly explain this for them.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If a practitioner perceives the body as being like empty space, this is the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).”
If a practitioner perceives that feeling cannot be found within, without, or between the two, this is the foundation of mindfulness of feeling;
if a practitioner knows that the mind exists only as a mere name, this is the foundation of mindfulness of mind;
if a practitioner finds neither wholesome dharmas nor unwholesome dharmas, this is the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas.
“Mañjuśrī, one should contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness in this way.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a practitioner contemplate the eightfold noble path?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If a practitioner perceives all phenomena as equal, non-dual, and without discrimination, this is called right view.
Perceiving all phenomena as beyond thought and without discrimination—by virtue of this perception—it is called right intention."
To see that all phenomena are without the characteristic of verbal expression, because one has skillfully cultivated the characteristic of the equality of speech—this is called right speech.
To see that all phenomena are without the characteristic of agency, because an agent cannot be apprehended—this is called right action.
Not discriminating between right livelihood and wrong livelihood, because of having well-cultivated the life of equanimity, this is called right livelihood.
Not giving rise to or producing any phenomena, because there is no activity, this is called right effort.
To have no recollection of any phenomena because the nature of all recollection is transcended is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
To see that the nature of all phenomena is eternally settled because it is non-dispersed, non-objectified, and ungraspable is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
"Mañjuśrī! A practitioner should contemplate the eightfold noble path in this way.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a practitioner contemplate the five faculties?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If a practitioner believes that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, because they have been thus from the very beginning, this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
When the mind dwells nowhere amidst all phenomena, because it remains detached from both the near and the far, this is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)."

To have no recollection of any phenomena because their nature is devoid of objective conditions, and thus not to bind one's mindfulness to those conditions—this is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
To have no conceptualization of any phenomena because dualistic dharmas cannot be apprehended—this is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
To see that all phenomena are eternally empty and free from the characteristic of arising—this is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Mañjuśrī!
A practitioner should contemplate the five faculties in this manner.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a practitioner contemplate the seven factors of enlightenment?”
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! When a practitioner is able to see that all phenomena are without recollection, this is called the mindfulness factor of enlightenment.”

If all phenomena—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—are neither selectable nor obtainable because they lack determinacy, this is called the factor-of-enlightenment of discernment (*pravicaya-sambodhyanga*).
If one does not grasp at the marks of the entire triple world because one has skillfully dismantled the triple world, this is called the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).

If one does not give rise to the mark of delight within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) because one has skillfully dismantled the mark of delight, this is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-sambodhyaṅga*).

If, among all phenomena, one eliminates the mind because the characteristics of objects cannot be apprehended, this is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
If all phenomena are unapprehendable because the characteristic of destruction is well-cultivated, this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

If one does not rely upon any phenomena, is neither greedy for nor attached to them, and attains a mind of equanimity by not perceiving any phenomena, this is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Mañjuśrī! A practitioner should contemplate the seven factors of enlightenment in this way.
If a practitioner can thus perceive the four noble truths, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the eightfold noble path, [they shall attain liberation].
One who possesses the five faculties and the seven factors of enlightenment— I say that such a person is one who has already crossed over,
reached the further shore, emerged onto dry land in a place of fearlessness, cast off the heavy burden, and removed all dust and defilement;
such a person is called one who possesses nothing, one who has no anxiety, and one who receives nothing.
These are called Arhats; these are called śramaṇas; these are called brāhmaṇas; these are called bhikṣus;
these are called those who have bathed and purified themselves; these are called the wise; these are called the liberated;
these are called the learned; these are called sons of the Buddha; these are called sons of Śākya; these are called those who have destroyed the thorns and briars.
This is called one who has removed the bolt; this is called one who has already crossed the moat; this is called one who has emerged from the search for desires;
this is called one who has opened the door-panels; this is called one who possesses the marks of excellence of the noble ones.
“Mañjuśrī! If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes such qualities as these, he is called a field of merit within the world of devas and humans, and he should receive offerings.”

Mañjuśrī! If this bhikṣu wishes not to consume in vain the offerings of the kingdom; wishes to destroy the net of Māra; wishes to cross the ocean of birth and death; wishes to attain nirvāṇa; wishes to be liberated from all suffering and affliction; and wishes to act as a field of merit for all devas, humans, and the world, he should diligently practice such dharmas as these.
When this Dharma was being taught, thirty-two thousand devas realized the true mark of all dharmas; each scattered heavenly *mandārava* flowers over the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

If a person hears such a Dharma as this, that person is called one who has truly gone forth; how much more so for one who believes and accepts it, recites and studies it, and practices according to what is taught?
World-Honored One!
"If there are those who hear this Dharma for even a moment, they shall be called those free from overweening pride.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One..."

When the dhāraṇī is expounded, by means of this dhāraṇī, all bodhisattvas shall attain unimpeded eloquence; they shall have no fear regarding any sounds, they shall be able to transform all phenomena into Buddha-dharmas, and they shall with faith and understanding realize that all phenomena are of a single characteristic.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall explain for you the Dharma-gate of the Immovable Seed-nature."
“Those bodhisattvas who succeed in entering this dharma-gate can, by means of the light of wisdom, illuminate all dharmas and swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"What is called the Dharma-gate of the lineage of the immovable state?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The minds of all sentient beings are fundamentally one; this is called the lineage."
“World-Honored One!
Why is this matter called ‘spiritual lineage’ (gotra)?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All sentient beings are entirely without mind, for the nature of conditions cannot be apprehended; this is called 'lineage' (gotra).
Mañjuśrī! All sentient beings are of one and the same measure; this is called 'seed' (bīja)."
“World-Honored One!
Why is this matter called ‘spiritual lineage’ (gotra)?
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings are equal in measure to space and ultimately return to non-obstruction; this is called the seed.
Mañjuśrī! All sentient beings are but a single sentient being; this is called the seed."
“World-Honored One!
Why is this matter called ‘spiritual lineage’ (gotra)?
“Mañjuśrī! [the Buddha replied.]

All sentient beings possess a single characteristic; they are ultimately unarisen and free from all names and designations, for neither identity nor difference can be apprehended. This is called the lineage (*gotra*).
“Mañjuśrī! Lust is the characteristic of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is this matter called the mark of immovability?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

Greed is the mark of immovability; it abides within the *dharmatā*. Because it does not abide, and because this greed is the nature of non-apprehensibility and is eternally detached, it is called the mark of immovability.
“Mañjuśrī! Anger is vajra.
“World-Honored One!”
"Why is this matter called 'vajra'? "Mañjuśrī!

Hatred cannot be severed and cannot be destroyed; it is like a vajra, which cannot be severed and cannot be destroyed. All dharmas are likewise: they cannot be severed and cannot be destroyed, because all dharmas are fundamentally indeterminate. Therefore, they are said to be 'like a vajra.'"
“Mañjuśrī! Ignorance is the nature of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is it that is called the nature of wisdom?

"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are free from wisdom and also free from delusion. Just as space possesses neither wisdom nor delusion, so too are all dharmas: they possess neither wisdom nor delusion. Wisdom, delusion, and the dharmas known by wisdom have been quiescent from the very beginning; therefore, this is called the locus of delusion and wisdom."
“Mañjuśrī! The aggregate of form is the station of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"Why is this matter called the 'immovable state'? "Mañjuśrī!

Just as the banner of the Lord of Devas has deep roots and is firmly established so that it cannot be shaken, all phenomena are likewise. Because they do not abide [in any fixed location], they dwell within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). These phenomena have no place from which they come and no place to which they go; they are neither grasped nor abandoned. Because they dwell in the state of non-dwelling, form is called the characteristic of immovability."
“Mañjuśrī! The aggregate of sensation is of the nature of cessation.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by this 'nature of cessation'? "Mañjuśrī,

because the nature and characteristics of all sensations (*vedanā*) are eternally quiescent, these sensations do not come from within or without, nor from the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below."
Why is this? If pleasant sensation were internal, all sentient beings would constantly experience pleasure;
if painful sensation were internal, all sentient beings would constantly experience suffering.
If the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant were internal, all sentient beings would experience only that which is neither painful nor pleasant. Mañjuśrī!

Now, all sensations truly exist neither internally, nor externally, nor in between the two; they do not exist in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below. Therefore, all sensations are like grass, trees, tiles, and stones—ultimately unborn and unceasing, and without marks. For this reason, sensation is called the mark of quiescence.
“Mañjuśrī! The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is the spiritual lineage (gotra).
“World-Honored One!”
"What is this matter called 'lineage' (gotra)?

"Mañjuśrī! These perceptions all arise from conceptualization and discrimination, being produced from the midst of falsehood. They are like an empty fist or a mirage; their fundamental nature is inherently detached. Therefore, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is called 'lineage.'"
"Mañjuśrī! The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is the spiritual lineage (gotra).
"World-Honored One!"
"What is this matter called 'lineage' (gotra)?

"Mañjuśrī! All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) transcend number and enter the number of the non-numerous; they are like the plantain tree, which ultimately has no core, for its intrinsic nature is thus. All dharmas are also like this: because they have no names and no intrinsic nature, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is therefore called 'lineage'."
“Mañjuśrī! The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is the lineage (gotra).
“World-Honored One!”
"What is this matter called 'spiritual lineage' (gotra)?
"Mañjuśrī! This consciousness is like an illusion;

it is without reality, without arising, and without birth. It is empty, signless, and without intrinsic nature. Just as when five fingers are applied to empty space, the empty space manifests without signs, for this reason the aggregate of consciousness is called the spiritual lineage."
“Mañjuśrī! Form is the spiritual lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
“What is meant by form being the lineage?
Mañjuśrī! It is like an image in a mirror:

though it can be seen with the eyes, it has no reality. All forms are likewise; though they are seen, they have no reality. They merely deceive the eye and deceive the mind, being false and unreal. For this reason, form is called the lineage.”
“Mañjuśrī, sound is the spiritual lineage (gotra).
“World-Honored One,
in what way is sound the spiritual lineage?”
“Mañjuśrī, all phenomena have no distinct characteristics; they are ultimately empty, like an echo in the mountains. Therefore, sound is the lineage.”
“Mañjuśrī! Fragrance is the spiritual lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is fragrance as the lineage (*gotra*)?

"Mañjuśrī! All phenomena (*dharma*) lack the characteristic of fragrance; because their nature is without cognition, they are empty like space. Since neither the nose, nor fragrance, nor olfactory consciousness can be apprehended, fragrance is thus the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī! Taste is the spiritual lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'taste as the lineage' (gotra)?

"Mañjuśrī, the nature of taste is itself the inconceivable nature; because it is unknowable and free from knowing, and because its self-nature is eternally detached, taste is thus called the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī! Contact is the spiritual lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'contact as the lineage' (gotra)?

"Mañjuśrī, contact is like space; its nature is inherently detached, being neither contacted nor combined. All phenomena are likewise so, because the body is well-dissolved and one is free from the characteristics of contact. Since a 'contactor' cannot be apprehended, contact is therefore the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī! The Dharma is the lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'dharmas as the lineage' (gotra)?
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are signless and mindless;

they are free from the nature of mind and free from names. Because they lack any fixed determination, they are all the characteristic of the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Therefore, dharmas are the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī, the earth is the spiritual lineage (gotra).
“World-Honored One,” [he replied].
"What is meant by 'earth as the lineage'?

"Mañjuśrī, all phenomena have neither the characteristic of hardness nor the characteristic of softness; it is through false conjunction that people regard them as hard. Therefore, earth is the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī, water is the spiritual lineage (gotra).
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]
"What is meant by water as the seed-nature?
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are neither moist nor conjoined; they are like a mirage, which contains no water. Therefore, water is the seed-nature."
“Mañjuśrī! Fire is the lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by fire being the lineage (*gotra*)? "Mañjuśrī!

All phenomena are without heat; they are free from the signs of false heat, for their intrinsic nature is quiescent and free from inversion. When one discerns them, they are truly neither fixed nor produced. For this reason, fire is called the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī! Wind is the lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
“What is meant by wind as the lineage (gotra)? “Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas are without obstruction or hindrance, without marks or intrinsic nature; because they are immovable and free from the characteristics of wind, wind is called the lineage.”
“Mañjuśrī! The Buddha is the spiritual lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by the Buddha being the lineage (gotra)? Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas are without awakening and without cognition, for they are free from the characteristics of cognition; therefore, the Buddha is called the lineage."
“Mañjuśrī! The Dharma is the lineage.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'dharmas as the lineage' (gotra)?

"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are indestructible and uncuttable; because they are free from destruction and cutting, they are signless, nameless, and without intrinsic nature, transcending the path of language. Therefore, dharmas are called the lineage."
"Mañjuśrī, the Saṃgha is the characteristic of immovability.
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by the Sangha having the characteristic of immovability? Mañjuśrī!

The noble assembly dwells in suchness, the dharma-nature, the limit of reality, and the equality of concentration and distraction; they dwell in all dharmas where wisdom and folly, and liberation and affliction are equal. Because their minds dwell nowhere—since a dwelling cannot be apprehended—the Sangha is called 'immovable nature.'"
“Mañjuśrī! The sphere of activity of all dharmas is called ‘immovable.
“World-Honored One!”
“What is this phenomenon called the ‘mark of immovability’? “Mañjuśrī!

Because all places of movement within space, places of inconceivable movement, and places of severed movement are without root, without distinction, and cannot be apprehended, therefore the place of movement of all phenomena is called the mark of immovability.”
“Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are without conditions; this is called the mark of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by this phenomenon being called the 'mark of immovability'? "Mañjuśrī!

All phenomena have no support, no place of abiding, no conditions, and no compliance; because they are free from all conditions, all phenomena are said to have no conditions—this is called the mark of immovability."
“Mañjuśrī! The characteristic of all phenomena being neither grasped nor abandoned is called the characteristic of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by this phenomenon being called the 'mark of immovability'? "Mañjuśrī!

All phenomena ultimately return to suchness and are identical to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). These phenomena cannot be grasped nor can they be abandoned; they are without seeking and without aspiration because all vows have been severed. From the very beginning, they have been eternally quiescent, their marks identical to empty space. Therefore, neither grasping nor abandoning is called the mark of immovability."
“Mañjuśrī! All phenomena being without fault is called the mark of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by this phenomenon being called the characteristic of immovability? "Mañjuśrī!

All phenomena are stainless and non-existent; they are pure and radiant like the cloudless sky. Because a fixed characteristic of any transgression cannot be found, all phenomena are faultless; this is called the characteristic of immovability."
“Mañjuśrī! All dharmas have no place of refuge; this is called the mark of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by this being called the mark of immovability? "Mañjuśrī!
Because all phenomena are empty and lack a fundamental basis, they have no place of refuge; therefore, having no place of refuge is called the mark of immovability."
“Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are without learning; this is called the mark of immovability.
“World-Honored One!”
"In what sense is this matter called the 'sign of immovability'? "Mañjuśrī!

The nature of all dharmas is beyond training; it should not be learned, should not be cultivated, should not be contemplated, should not be recollected, should not be dwelled upon, should not be initiated, should not be practiced, should not be abandoned, should not be realized, should not be spoken, should not be uttered, should not be sought, should not be explained, should not be grasped, should not be relinquished, should not be separated from, and should not be eliminated."
Why is this? Mañjuśrī! Because all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are ultimately detached;

from the very beginning they have been non-appropriative and are eternally characterized by relinquishment (*tyāga*). All phenomena (*dharma*) are beyond the reach of wisdom and beyond the reach of folly; therefore, the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is called the mark of immovability (*aniñjya-lakṣaṇa*).
