At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on the mark of immovability.
The Buddha said:
"You who delight in eloquent exposition,
you may now speak. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One!..."
"All sentient beings attain bodhi; this is called the mark of immovability.
"Mañjuśrī! Why is this matter called the mark of immovability?"
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are without direction and without attainment; all sentient beings enter into the nature of bodhi. For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings attain bodhi.”
Furthermore, bodhi is not a characteristic that can be attained. Why is this?
Because the nature of sentient beings is itself bodhi; therefore, all sentient beings attain bodhi, which is called the characteristic of immovability.
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings fully accomplish all wisdom; this is called the mark of immovability.
“Mañjuśrī! [The Buddha said:]
"What is meant by this 'characteristic of immovability'?
"World-Honored One!

All sentient beings are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they enter into the equality of the Tathāgata. Since, from the very beginning, their nature as the essence of all-encompassing wisdom is identical, it is called the characteristic of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); this is the mark of immovability. “Mañjuśrī!”
"In what sense is this matter called the 'mark of immovability'?
"World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of the term 'site of enlightenment' (bodhimaṇḍa)?"

“Mañjuśrī! All dharmas have the characteristic of quiescence, the characteristic of non-arising, the characteristic of non-existence, and the characteristic of being ungraspable; this is the meaning of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).”
“World-Honored One!
Do all sentient beings not enter this site of enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Therefore, World-Honored One, all sentient beings are the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); this is called the mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena; this is called the mark of immovability.
“Mañjuśrī! [The Buddha said:]
"What is meant by this phenomenon being called the mark of immovability?
"World-Honored One!

Because all sentient beings are inexhaustible, unborn, and unceasing; because their nature is detached from having a nature; and because they have entered into the patience of equality—therefore, all sentient beings attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, which is called the mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
That all sentient beings attain unimpeded eloquence is called the mark of immovability.
“How is this matter called the mark of immovability?”
“World-Honored One!
All the eloquence possessed by all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions cannot be found when sought. Why is this so? Because...”
Because they all enter into the dharma of impartiality and unimpeded eloquence.
World-Honored One!

All that is delightfully expounded is by nature detached, because it lacks determination and because it is non-existent; therefore, all sentient beings attain unimpeded eloquence, which is called the mark of immovability.
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings shall attain a dhāraṇī named ‘the mark of immovability. “Mañjuśrī!”
“What is meant by this phenomenon being called the ‘mark of immovability’?
“World-Honored One!

Because all sentient beings, by means of the mark of a sentient being, can maintain forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas—and because they grasp at marks through false, unreal recollections, thoughts, and discriminations—all sentient beings thereby attain a dharani called the ‘mark of immovability.’”
“World-Honored One!
That all sentient beings attain a mind of loving-kindness is called the mark of immovability.
“Mañjuśrī! [The Buddha continued:]
"What is meant by this 'characteristic of immovability'?
"World-Honored One!

All sentient beings lack the nature of a sentient being; from the very beginning, they have neither anger nor loving-kindness. Because they attain the equality of anger and loving-kindness and are free from discrimination, all sentient beings thus possess a mind of loving-kindness—this is called the characteristic of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are fully endowed with great compassion; this is called the mark of immovability.
“Mañjuśrī! [The Buddha continued:]
"What is meant by this state being called the 'mark of immovability'?
"World-Honored One!

All sentient beings possess the mark of non-arising and non-activity; they all enter into the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharma and do not depart from the nature of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because affliction and compassion are non-discriminatory, all sentient beings thus accomplish great compassion. This is what is called the mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings attain a samādhi called ‘the mark of immovability.
“Mañjuśrī! [The Buddha replied.]
"What is meant by 'the characteristic of immovability'?
"World-Honored One!
The nature of all sentient beings is eternally settled, because it is free from all conditions."
If sentient beings were to have cognition arise from conditions, or if cognition were to arise within conditions, it would not be called true cognition. Why is this?
Because all cognitions are impermanent from moment to moment and are ultimately empty. Therefore, all sentient beings achieve a samādhi called the "mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas have fully accomplished desire; this is called the mark of immovability. “Mañjuśrī!”
"Why is this matter called the mark of immovability?
"World-Honored One!
It is because all Buddhas have entered the dharma of the equality of desire, and because they have distanced themselves from contention and attained penetration into the nature of desire."
World-Honored One!
Greed is itself bodhi. Why is this so?
Knowing the true nature of desire is called bodhi; therefore, all Buddhas are said to be fully accomplished in desire, which is termed the "unmoving mark.
World-Honored One!
"All Buddhas have fully accomplished anger; this is called the mark of immovability.
"Mañjuśrī, why is this matter called the mark of immovability?"
“World-Honored One!

When all Buddhas speak of the faults of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they abide in the equality of hatred and penetrate the nature of hatred; therefore, this is called ‘all Buddhas being fully accomplished in hatred,’ which is termed the mark of immovability.”
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas achieve delusion; this is called the mark of immovability. “Mañjuśrī!”
"What is this phenomenon called the 'mark of immovability'?
"World-Honored One!

All Buddhas are able to deliver all sentient beings who are attached to names; they abide in the equality of ignorance and have thoroughly penetrated the nature of ignorance. Therefore, it is said that all Buddhas accomplish ignorance—this is called the mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas have fully accomplished the view of a self-body; this is called the mark of immovability. “Mañjuśrī!”
"What is meant by this state being called the 'mark of immovability'? "World-Honored One!

All Buddhas abide within the nature of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Within all dharmas, they do not regress, do not fear, and do not move, abiding ultimately and completely. Because they do not dwell in any phenomena, they penetrate and know that the view of a self is unborn, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature. For this reason, all Buddhas fully accomplish the view of a self; this is called the mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas are of false views; this is called the mark of immovability. “Mañjuśrī!”
"What is meant by this being called the mark of immovability?
"World-Honored One!

All Buddhas and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are false, deceptive, and unreal. Because they have realized the equality of the nature of wrong views, for this reason all Buddhas are themselves wrong views; this is called the mark of immovability."
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas abide in the four inversions, the five hindrances, the five desires, and the three poisons, yet they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called the mark of immovability.”
“Mañjuśrī! Why is this matter called the ‘sign of immovability’?
“World-Honored One!”
“The nature of a dwelling place is itself a non-dwelling place. “Mañjuśrī!
What is the meaning of ‘non-dwelling place’?”
“World-Honored One!
Those who do not abide are those characterized by regression, movement, and returning; these are all ordinary worldlings.
All Buddhas, however, dwell peacefully within the equality of desire, hatred, ignorance, the four inversions, the five hindrances, and the five desires.”

Because these Buddhas abide in the nature of greed and desire, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; because they abide in the nature of anger, delusion, the four inversions, the five hindrances, and the five desires, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, all Buddhas abide within the four inversions, the five hindrances, the five desires, and the three poisons, yet they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the mark of immovability.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince:
“If someone were to ask you:
‘The severing of all unwholesome dharmas and the accomplishment of all wholesome dharmas is called the Tathāgata.’”
"How would you answer? Mañjuśrī replied,
"World-Honored One!"
If someone were to ask me, "Who is it that has severed all unwholesome dharmas and accomplished all wholesome dharmas who is called the Tathāgata? I would answer them thus:
"Good son!..."

You should first draw near to virtuous friends and cultivate the path of goodness; regarding all phenomena, there is neither conjunction nor dispersion. Do not grasp, do not abandon; do not rely upon them, do not seek them; do not elevate them, do not debase them; do not strive for them, do not search for them, and do not form wishes for them. Do not discriminate among phenomena as superior, middling, or inferior. Only then will you know the inconceivable sphere of practice, the sphere of non-practice, the sphere of the cessation of practice, and the sphere of the Buddhas' practice.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“When you answer in this way, what meaning are you answering? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
To answer in such a manner as I have done is called ‘answering nothing.
World-Honored One!”
"If the Buddha were seated at the site of enlightenment, would he perceive any dharma that arises or ceases?
The Buddha said, "No."
“World-Honored One!
If a dharma is neither born nor extinguished, can that dharma be said to sever all unwholesome dharmas and accomplish all wholesome dharmas?”
The Buddha said,
“No. [He asked,] “World-Honored One!”

If dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, and one neither abandons any unwholesome dharmas nor accomplishes any wholesome dharmas, what is there to be seen, what is there to be abandoned, what is there to be realized, what is there to be cultivated, and what is there to be attained?

When these words were spoken, ten thousand devaputras in the void scattered celestial blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses over the Buddha and Mañjuśrī; they all descended to prostrate at the feet of the Buddha and Mañjuśrī, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

Mañjuśrī is named Unobstructed Śrī; Mañjuśrī is named Non-dual Śrī, named Remainderless Śrī, named Non-existent Śrī, named Suchness Śrī, Dharmatā Śrī, Reality-limit Śrī, Supreme Śrī, Exalted Śrī, and Unsurpassed Śrī.
Mañjuśrī said to the devaputras:
"Stop, stop, O devaputras!
"You should not grasp at signs or engage in conceptual discrimination; I do not perceive any phenomena as superior, middling, or inferior, contrary to what you have said.
Mañjuśrī replied, "I am the śrī of desire, the śrī of hatred, and the śrī of delusion; for this reason, I am named Mañjuśrī."
"O sons of the gods!

I do not emerge from desire, hatred, or delusion; it is ordinary people who, by discriminating among phenomena, seek to transcend them and reach a point of arrival. For bodhisattvas, there is no transgression, no emergence, no departure, and no arrival regarding phenomena."
The devaputras asked:
"Does a bodhisattva not reach the ten stages, and does he not attain the Buddha-dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"What do you think, sons of the gods?
Can an illusory person reach the ten stages or attain the Buddha-dharma?
The sons of the gods replied:
“Even an illusory person has no place of abiding; how much less so for one who proceeds from this stage to another stage.
Mañjuśrī said, “O sons of the gods!...”
"All dharmas are like illusions; they neither go nor come, neither pass away nor emerge, neither arrive nor reach.
The devaputras asked, "Should you not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O sons of the gods!
What do you think?"
“Can an ordinary person whose mind is shrouded by craving sit at the site of enlightenment and attain all-knowledge?
The sons of the gods replied, “No.”
The devaputras said:
"Mañjuśrī! Are you now an ordinary person whose mind is obscured by desire?"
Mañjuśrī said: “So it is, so it is!
I am an ordinary person; I arise from desire, I arise from hatred, and I arise from delusion. I am a follower of external paths and one who practices erroneously.”
The devaputras asked:
"For what reason do you say of yourself:
'I am an ordinary person, arisen from desire, arisen from hatred, and arisen from delusion'?"

Mañjuśrī said: "The nature of this greed, anger, and delusion cannot be found even if one searches throughout the ten directions. Because I abide in this nature by means of the dharma of non-abiding, I say that I am an ordinary person covered by the three poisons."
“Mañjuśrī! Why are you called a non-Buddhist (tīrthika)? Mañjuśrī replied:
"I shall never go to the paths of the outsiders, for the nature of all such paths cannot be apprehended; thus, I am 'outside' of all paths.
The sons of the gods asked:
"In what sense are you a practitioner of heterodox ways?"
Mañjuśrī said: "I already know that all dharmas are perverse, false, and unreal; therefore, I am one who practices what is perverse."
When this Dharma was being spoken, ten thousand devaputras heard these words and all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Each of them spoke thus:

“All these sentient beings have gained a great benefit in hearing these true and authentic vajra phrases; how much more so for those who, having heard them, believe and understand, receive and uphold them, read and recite them, explain them to others, and practice according to the teaching—they shall attain unimpeded eloquence, obtain the illumination of true wisdom regarding all dharmas, skillfully expound the single characteristic and single gate of all dharmas, and be able to show sentient beings that all dharmas are indeed the Buddha-dharma.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower-Play-Wisdom addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will expound the Dharma-gate of entering the wisdom of sounds, so that future bodhisattvas, upon hearing such a teaching, shall not be startled or terrified; and so that they may know the ultimate nature of all sounds without doubt or regret, remaining unobstructed regarding all sounds.”
The Buddha said:
"Stop, stop!
What is the use of asking about this matter?"
This Dharma gate of the wisdom of entering sounds and voices should not be taught before bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds. Why is this?
Because those who have newly resolved their minds are unable to understand, unable to know, and unable to contemplate it.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters this dharma-gate of the wisdom of sounds, even if someone were to revile, slander, and disparage them with harsh speech for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, that person would give rise to no resentment or anger.
If a person were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they would not give rise to a mind of attachment.
Just as an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward any object of attachment, nor gives rise to a mind of aversion toward any object of aversion.
"Good son!

This Bodhisattva Dharmamukha Ghoṣaprajñā has transcended the eight worldly dharmas—gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—and his mind is unshakable, like Sumeru, the king of mountains."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower-Play-Wisdom again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that you will certainly explain for us the Dharma-gate of Entering the Wisdom of Sounds. When future Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma-gate, they shall know their own faults and also instruct others."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Flower-Play Wisdom:
“Good son! Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.”
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Flower-Play-Wisdom:

"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing sounds of desire, conceives the notion of fault and transgression, and upon hearing sounds of freedom from desire, conceives the notion of benefit, they are not training in the Buddha-dharma."
If, upon hearing sounds of anger and hatred, one conceives thoughts of fault and transgression, yet upon hearing sounds free from anger and hatred, one conceives thoughts of benefit;

or if, upon hearing sounds of ignorance and delusion, one conceives thoughts of fault and transgression, yet upon hearing sounds free from ignorance and delusion, one conceives thoughts of benefit—then this is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one conceives a notion of delight toward sounds of few desires and a notion of obstruction toward sounds of many desires, this is not practicing the Dharma-gate of sounds.
If one conceives a notion of delight toward sounds of contentment and a notion of obstruction toward sounds of discontent, this is not practicing the Dharma-gate of sounds.

If one conceives a notion of delight toward subtle sounds and voices while conceiving a notion of obstruction toward coarse sounds and voices, then this is not practicing the Dharma-gate of sounds and voices.
If one delights in sounds and voices that are quiet and secluded while obstructing those that are clamorous and noisy, then this is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one conceives the notion of benefit toward the sound of patience and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of anger, then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one conceives the notion of benefit toward the sound of diligence and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of laziness, then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
To conceive the notion of benefit toward sounds of meditative concentration and the notion of obstruction toward sounds of distraction is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To conceive the notion of benefit toward sounds of wisdom and the notion of obstruction toward sounds of ignorance is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
If one delights in sounds that are near to the Path and is obstructed by sounds that are distant from the Path, then one is not training in the Dharma-gate of sound.
If one perceives faults in saṃsāra and perceives benefits in nirvāṇa, then one does not enter the Dharma-gate of sound.
To feel joy regarding the far shore and obstruction regarding this shore is not to study the Dharma-gate of sounds.
To give rise to the notion of obstruction toward the sounds of villages and the notion of joy toward the sounds of secluded places is not to study the Dharma-gate of sounds.

If one conceives a notion of delight toward sounds uttered by those who practice alone, and a notion of obstruction toward sounds uttered by those who practice in a group, then one is not training in the Dharma-gate of sounds.

If one conceives a notion of delight toward sounds uttered by bhikṣus, and a notion of obstruction toward sounds uttered by laypeople (avadātavasana), then one is not training in the Dharma-gate of sounds.
If one delights in proper deportment and is hindered by improper deportment, then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one delights in pure conduct and is hindered by impure conduct, then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one delights in solitary practice and is hindered by mixed practice, then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one delights in the practice of detachment from desire and is hindered by the practice of sensual desire, then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
To take delight in thoughts free from hatred while being obstructed by thoughts of hatred is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To take delight in thoughts free from delusion while being obstructed by thoughts of delusion is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To take delight in emptiness while being obstructed by existence is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To take delight in the signless while being obstructed by signs is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To delight in the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) while being hindered by the conditioned (*sabhisaṃskāra*) is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To delight in the conduct of a bodhisattva while being hindered by the conduct of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
If one speaks of the faults and transgressions of a bodhisattva, one distances oneself from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and also incurs the retribution of karmic obstacles.

If one speaks of the failings in the deportment of a bodhisattva, one distances oneself from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; furthermore, if a bodhisattva conceives a sense of inferiority toward another bodhisattva while conceiving a sense of superiority toward themselves, they harm themselves and also incur the retribution of karmic obstacles.
If a bodhisattva wishes to instruct another bodhisattva, they should first conceive of that person as a Buddha and only then instruct them.
If a bodhisattva does not wish to abandon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should not give rise to thoughts of contempt or anger toward other bodhisattvas.
"Good son!

There is no loss of merit comparable to that of slighting or becoming angry with other bodhisattvas. Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to protect their meritorious roots and attain unobstructed wisdom regarding all dharmas should, three times each day and night, pay homage to all bodhisattvas who seek the path of the Buddha."
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the sound of lustful desire and the voice of the Buddha are equal and without difference.”
The voice of malice is equal to the voice of the Buddha; the voice of ignorance is equal to the voice of the Buddha; the voices of non-Buddhists are equal to the voice of the Buddha;
the voice of few desires is equal to the voice of many desires; the voice of contentment is equal to the voice of discontent;
the subtle voice is equal to the coarse voice; and the voice of delighting in solitude [is equal to all].
The sounds of various musical instruments; the sounds of this shore and the sounds of the other shore;
distant sounds and near sounds; the sounds of birth and death and the sounds of nirvāṇa; the sounds of villages and the sounds of secluded places;
the sounds of generosity and the sounds of stinginess; the sounds of upholding the precepts and the sounds of violating the precepts.
The sounds of [the afflictions] such as sound and so forth; the sounds of patience and the sounds of anger; the sounds of diligence and the sounds of laziness;
the sounds of meditative concentration and the sounds of distracted mind; the sounds of wisdom and the sounds of delusion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Puṣpavikrīḍitamatī asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī,
“By what causes and conditions are they all equal?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven!
What do you think?
Of the sounds of desire, which one is real?”
The devaputra said,
"The sound of desire is empty, like an echo. Mañjuśrī said:
“You know that the Buddha’s voice is likewise;
how is it so? The devaputra replied, “It does not emerge from emptiness, nor is it like the nature of an echo.”
Mañjuśrī said, “For these reasons, I say that both sounds are equal.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"When you previously dwelt on the stage of the initial resolve and had not yet entered into the characteristics of these dharmas, what obstructing offenses did you commit?
Speak of them now."
"In future ages, those bodhisattvas who use mere conventional names, upon hearing what you have said regarding the offenses that constitute obstacles, shall protect themselves accordingly.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
saying, "So be it, World-Honored One!"

I shall now speak of the offenses that constitute obstacles; those who hear this should feel concern and fear, yet they will also be able to extinguish the offenses of their karmic hindrances and attain unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena.
“World-Honored One!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Siṃhanāda-dundubhisvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān!”
The lifespan of that Buddha was one hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* years, and he delivered sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

His land was named Thousand Radiances; the trees of that land were all composed of the seven treasures, and from those trees issued forth such sounds of the Dharma as the sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-existence, and the sound of the absence of grasping at signs. By means of these sounds of the various Dharmas, he caused sentient beings to attain the Way.

When that Buddha Siṃhanāda-dundubhisvara-rāja first preached the Dharma in his initial assembly, nine hundred and ninety million śrāvaka disciples all attained arhatship; their outflows were exhausted, they had laid down their heavy burdens, they had achieved their own benefit, they had ended the fetters of existence, and they were liberated through right knowledge.

The assembly of bodhisattvas also numbered ninety-nine billion; all had attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), were able to skillfully enter various dharma-gates, and had attended upon and made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas. They were likewise praised by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, were able to deliver hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable sentient beings, were able to give rise to immeasurable dharani-gates, and were able to manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samadhi-gates;
as well as other newly resolved bodhisattvas who were beyond counting.
The adornments of that Buddha’s land are immeasurable and cannot be fully described.
After that Buddha had completed his dwelling in the world and his work of teaching and transforming beings, he entered parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Following his passing, the Dharma remained for sixty thousand years, after which the sounds of the Dharma no longer issued forth from the trees.

"At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Nandendriya who served as a Dharma teacher; he was upright and dignified, maintaining his majestic deportment without fail while not abandoning worldly ways."
At that time, all sentient beings possessed sharp faculties and delighted in hearing profound discourses.

Before the assembly, the Dharma Master Xigan did not praise few desires, contentment, subtle conduct, or solitary dwelling; rather, he taught the assembly the true mark of all dharmas, saying: "The nature of all dharmas is the very nature of greed; the nature of greed is the very nature of all dharmas. The nature of hatred is the very nature of all dharmas; the nature of delusion is the very nature of all dharmas."

The Dharma Master Xigen used these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings; the practices of all these beings were of a single characteristic, with none criticizing or disputing one another. In the path they practiced, their minds were free from anger and delusion. Because of these causes and conditions of being unobstructed by anger, they swiftly attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) and became firm and indestructible within the Buddha-dharma.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, there was another bhikṣu, a Dharma-master practicing the bodhisattva path, named Jayamati.
That bhikṣu Jayamati upheld the prohibitive precepts, attained the four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations, and practiced the twelve dhūtas.”
“World-Honored One!
This bhikṣu Jeta has several disciples whose minds are fickle and who delight in seeing the faults of others.
World-Honored One!”

Later, on one occasion, the Bodhisattva Jayamati entered a village to beg for alms and mistakenly arrived at the house of a disciple of Nandika. Seeing the son of a householder who was the master of the household, he went to him, prepared a seat, and sat down. He praised the son of the householder for having few desires, being content, and practicing subtle conduct; he spoke words regarding the faults of profitlessness and extolled those who stay far from the crowd and delight in solitary practice.

Furthermore, before the son of the householder, he spoke of the faults of the Dharma Master Nandika: "This bhikṣu is not truthful; he teaches and transforms sentient beings with false views. He is a practitioner of mixed conduct, saying that there is no obstacle to lust, no obstacle to anger, and no obstacle to delusion, and that all dharmas are without obstacle."
This son of a householder, possessing sharp faculties, attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and addressed the venerable bhikṣu Jitāmitra:
"Do you know what kind of phenomenon lust is?"
Jayaśas said: "Householder!
I know that sensual desire is an affliction."
The son of a householder said:
"Venerable Sir!
Does this affliction exist within or without?"
Jayaśas said:
"It is neither within nor without.
[The other asked: "Venerable sir!"
If desire does not exist internally, nor externally, nor in the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—then it is unborn.
If it is unborn, how can one speak of it as being either defiled or pure?
At that time, the bhikṣu Jayamati, filled with anger and displeasure, rose from his seat and departed, saying these words:
"This bhikṣu Nandika deludes many people with the practice of false speech."
Because this person has not studied the dharma-gate of entering into sounds, they feel joy upon hearing the voice of a Buddha, yet feel anger upon hearing the voice of a non-Buddhist;
they feel joy toward the voice of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), yet feel anger toward the voice of that which is not pure conduct.
Because they have not trained in entering the dharma-gate of sounds, they rejoice in pure sounds and feel aversion toward defiled sounds.
Because they have not trained in entering the dharma-gate of sounds, they rejoice in the sounds of the noble path and are obstructed by the sounds of ordinary beings.
Because they have not trained in entering the dharma-gate of sounds, they take pleasure in pleasant sounds and feel aversion toward painful sounds.

Because they have not trained in entering the dharma-gate of sounds, they take pleasure in the sounds of those who have left the household life and feel aversion toward the sounds of those who remain at home.
Because they have not trained in entering the dharma-gate of sounds, they take delight in supramundane sounds while being obstructed by mundane sounds.
Because they have not trained in entering the dharma-gate of sounds, they conceive the notion of benefit regarding generosity, while conceiving the notion of obstruction regarding stinginess.
Because they do not study the Buddha-dharma,
they conceive the notion of benefit regarding the observance of precepts and the notion of obstruction regarding the violation of precepts.
This is because they do not study the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu Jayamati, having left his dwelling and returned to where he stayed, saw the bodhisattva Nandika among the assembly of monks and said to the people:

"This bhikṣu frequently teaches and transforms sentient beings with many false and erroneous views, namely: 'Sensual desire is not an obstacle; hatred is not an obstacle; delusion is not an obstacle; all dharmas are not obstacles.'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nandendriya thought to himself:

"This bhikṣu will surely now give rise to obstructive karmic offenses. I shall now explain such profound Dharma to him, even to the point of causing him to create the causes and conditions for practicing the auxiliary dharmas of the path to enlightenment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nandendriya, before the assembly of monks, spoke these verses:
“Lust is nirvāṇa; hatred and delusion are likewise so.
Within these three things, there lies the immeasurable path of the Buddha.”
If there is someone who discriminates between greed, hatred, and delusion,
that person is as far from the Buddha as heaven is from earth.
Awakening and greed are one and not two.
All enter a single Dharma-gate, equal and without distinction.
When ordinary people hear this, they are terrified; they are far removed from the Buddha-way.
Yet, because their greed and desire neither arise nor cease, they cannot cause their minds to be afflicted.
If a person possesses the notion of a self, And possesses the notion of one who perceives,
That person, driven by craving, Will enter into hell.
The true nature of craving Is itself the nature of the Buddha-dharma.
The true nature of the Buddha-dharma is also the nature of desire;
these two dharmas have one and the same characteristic, which is called "signlessness.
If one can understand it in this way, one shall become a guide for the world.

If someone makes such discriminations as "this one observes the precepts" or "that one violates them," and because of being intoxicated by their observance of the precepts, they look down upon others,
that person has no awakening, nor do they possess the Buddha-dharma.
If one merely abides established within the view of something to be attained,
and while dwelling in a secluded place, holds oneself in high esteem and looks down upon others,
such a person will not even attain rebirth in heaven, let alone attain Bodhi.
All this arises from attachment to emptiness and dwelling in false views;
thus, false views and bodhi are equal and without distinction.
They differ only through the enumeration of names and the use of speech.
If a person thoroughly penetrates this, they will be close to bodhi.
To conceptually differentiate the defilements of affliction is itself the attachment to the view of purity;
there is no bodhi or Buddha-dharma for one who dwells within the view of attainment.
If one is greedily attached to the Buddha-dharma, one is far removed from the Buddha-dharma;
because one craves the unimpeded dharma, one instead undergoes suffering and affliction.
If a person is free from discrimination, [they are free from] greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because one enters into the nature of the three poisons, one then perceives bodhi;
such a person draws near to the Buddha-way and swiftly attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If one sees that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are different from unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), [one does not perceive bodhi].
Such a person will never attain liberation from conditioned phenomena;
yet if they know that these two natures are identical, they will surely become the Honored One among men.
The Buddha does not perceive *bodhi*, nor does he perceive the Buddha-dharma.
Because they do not cling to any phenomena, they subdue Māra and realize the Buddha-way.
If you wish to deliver sentient beings, do not discriminate their nature;
all sentient beings are identical with nirvāṇa.
If one can see in this way, then one shall attain Buddhahood.
One whose mind is not tranquil yet manifests the appearance of tranquility is,
among gods and humans, a great thief indeed.
Such a person has no bodhi, nor do they possess the Buddha-dharma.
If one makes such a vow as "I shall become a Buddha," such an ordinary person is led away by the power of ignorance.
The Buddha-dharma is profound and pure, comparable to empty space;
herein there is nothing to be grasped, nor is there anything to be abandoned.
The Buddha does not attain the path of Buddhahood, nor does he deliver sentient beings.
Ordinary people forcibly engage in conceptual discrimination, thinking, "I shall become a Buddha to deliver sentient beings.
Such persons are then very far indeed from the Buddha-dharma.
If they perceive the suffering of sentient beings, they themselves become sufferers of that suffering.
Sentient beings are no sentient beings, yet one speaks of there being sentient beings;
if one dwells within the mark of sentient beings, then there is no bodhi.
If a person perceives sentient beings as such, this is ultimate liberation.
Free from lust, anger, and delusion—know such a one to be a leader of the world.
If a person perceives sentient beings but does not perceive what is non-sentient, they do not attain the reality of the Buddha-dharma; for the Buddha is of the same nature as all sentient beings.
If one can know it thus, one shall be a leader of the world.
If a person wishes to attain Buddhahood, they must not destroy the nature of desire;
for the very nature of desire is the merit of all Buddhas.
If a person wishes to resolve their mind, following the path to enlightenment,
they must not harbor the discrimination that the mind is different from enlightenment;
for the resolution of the mind is itself enlightenment— one who knows this is a leader of the world.
If one speaks of the evil of non-Buddhists, And praises the Buddha as the most honored in the world, These two statements are not different; One who knows this is a leader of the world.
If a person seeks bodhi, That person has no bodhi.
If one perceives the marks of awakening, one is far removed from awakening.
Awakening is not awakening; both Buddha and non-Buddha—if one knows them to be of a single mark, such a person is a guide for the world.
If a person forms this thought, "I shall deliver sentient beings," they are immediately attached to the mark of sentient beings.
Such a person has no bodhi, nor do they possess the Buddha-dharma; they abide within the view of existence.
Greed has no interior or exterior, nor does it abide in any direction;
it is a conceptualization of empty phenomena, by which ordinary beings are consumed.
It is like a phantom, a mirage, or an echo; it is like a dream or the son of a barren woman.
All afflictions are thus; they are definitively unobtainable.
Because they do not know them to be empty, ordinary beings are deluded and confused.
If one seeks the nature of afflictions, those very afflictions are the Path.
If someone discriminates, thinking "this is the path" or "this is not the path," that person will ultimately never attain the non-conceptual bodhi.
Ordinary beings who fear the Buddha-dharma remain very far from it.
If one does not doubt the dharma of emptiness, this person attains bodhi.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are themselves unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*);
their numericality cannot be apprehended, and because they are non-numerical, they are unconditioned.
If, by means of the bodhicitta, one is self-exalting and fearless,
thinking "I shall become a Buddha," such a person possesses neither bodhi nor the Buddha-dharma;
they have departed from the precious seal of bodhi.
If there are those who merely recite the sutras, forming conceptual distinctions through mental recollection,
yet do not deeply contemplate their profound meaning, but instead act only out of greed for fame and profit,
thinking to themselves, "I shall surely become a Buddha"— of this they have no doubt that they will indeed achieve it.
Craving only for fame and profit, though one recites the scriptures and dwells in seclusion,
practicing the conduct of few desires, one is still dragged away by a greedy mind.
If you wish to abandon and distance yourself from greed, yet cannot distance yourself from greed, [you remain bound].
If one realizes the true nature of greed, that person can leave greed behind.
Without attaining the reality-limit (dharmatā), though one observes the precepts for a long night and attains various unimpeded dhyānas,
one does not enter the flavor of the Buddha-dharma.
Knowing that phenomena have no intrinsic nature, one does not destroy any phenomena;
by not speaking of precepts as either "precepts" or "non-precepts," one attains liberation from views of existence.
Because there is no intrinsic nature in the observance of precepts, one understands the dharma of observing precepts.
Knowing the characteristics of the precepts in this way, one shall never violate them.
The Dharma-kings, the Buddhas, possess an inconceivable treasury of Dharma;
through the power of immeasurable skillful means, they guide all sentient beings.
By means of the dharma-gate of the single characteristic, they cause [beings] to enter the path of quiescent extinction.
When ordinary people hear the Buddha’s teaching that there is no self and no phenomena,
and that the single characteristic is empty of intrinsic nature, they do not believe it and fall into a deep pit.
Though a layperson enjoying sensual desires, if they hear this Dharma without fear,
they surpass those practitioners of dhūta who remain stuck in views of existence.
The Buddhas of the ten directions in the present are benefiting all worlds.
Knowing that all phenomena are like space, they have all attained bodhi.
If there are those without wisdom who delight in the conceptual differentiation of phenomena,
upon hearing this true Dharma, they will give rise to doubt and fear.
"For immeasurable kalpas, this person shall fully undergo all portions of suffering.

When these verses on the Dharma were spoken, thirty thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and eighteen thousand people were liberated through the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
Immediately the earth split open, and the bhikṣu Śreṇika fell into the great hell.
Due to these karmic obstructions and the causes and conditions of his offenses, for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas he underwent various bitter sufferings in the great hells;
upon emerging from the hells, he was constantly slandered for seven hundred and forty thousand lifetimes, and for several hundreds of thousands of kalpas he did not even hear the name of the Buddha.

From that time onward, he again encountered Buddhas, left the household life to study the Path, yet lacked the resolve and joy [for it]; for six hundred and thirty thousand lifetimes, he constantly turned away from the Path and returned to secular life;
furthermore, due to the remaining karmic obstructions of his past deeds, his faculties remained dull and obtuse for several hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
“World-Honored One!

At that time, the Dharma Master Nandendriya is now, to the east, beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, in a land named Ratnavyūha, where he has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and is currently present as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Jayasūryaprabhatejorāja.”
That Bhikṣu Viśeṣamati was none other than my own self.
World-Honored One!

Before I had entered this gateway of the Dharma-characteristics, I experienced such suffering, the suffering of discrimination, and the suffering of perversion. Therefore, those who have resolved for Bodhicitta, or those who have resolved for the Hīnayāna, who do not wish to give rise to such karmic obstructions and sins, and who do not wish to undergo such afflictions and distress, should not reject or oppose the Buddha-Dharma; there is no place where anger or obstruction can arise.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“What benefit do you derive from hearing these verses? Mañjuśrī replied,
“World-Honored One!”

Once I have exhausted these karmic obstacles and transgressions, by virtue of the causes and conditions of hearing these verses, in every place where I am born, I shall possess keen faculties and wisdom, attain profound dharma-patience and definitive patience, and skillfully expound the profound Dharma.
“Mañjuśrī! By whose power are you able to remember such immeasurable, incalculable eons of karmic causes and conditions for offenses?
“World-Honored One!”
Whatever the bodhisattvas think, whatever they speak, and whatever they contemplate—all these are the spiritual power of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because all dharmas arise from the Buddha.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If one attains the ten powers of a Buddha, and if there is one who hears this sutra, they are equal and no different;
if one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, and if there is one who hears this sutra, they likewise are equal and no different."
Mañjuśrī said: “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, those who hear this sutra will obtain the benefit of immeasurable and inconceivable merit.”
“Mañjuśrī! It is so, it is so!
By hearing this sutra, one obtains immeasurable and inconceivable benefits of merit; however, the Buddha does not explain them in detail.”
"Why is this? Because those who do not cultivate the path and lack diligence—such evil persons as these—will be unable to believe and accept this teaching of benefit when they hear it.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Please protect and mind this sutra during the final five hundred years of the future age, so that it may be widely proclaimed and circulated, and all may receive and uphold it, such that Māras or celestial Māras shall find no opportunity to gain the upper hand.”

At that time, because the Buddha wished to protect and keep this Dharma in mind, he looked around to his left and right; immediately, immeasurable lands in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shook in six ways. In this way, he protected and kept this sutra in mind, and the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise protected and kept this sutra in mind.

When this sutra was being preached, immeasurable sentient beings in lands throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; how much more so those who had attained the stage of no-more-learning among the śrāvakas, and how much more so those dwelling on the stages of learning?
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what name should this sutra be known, and how should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Ānanda, “This sūtra is named ‘The Non-Practice of All Dharmas. Having spoken this sūtra, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince,

Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Siṃhavikrāntagāmin Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Puṣpavicitramati Devaputra, and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as Ānanda, devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had taught, were all greatly delighted.
